note: The adjective follows the noun in this fixed greeting, the reverse of everyday Polish word order. Used from morning until early evening; after dark Poles switch to 'Dobry wieczór'.
A first-person verb, not a noun: you are literally saying 'I thank'. The root came into Old Polish from Czech, which borrowed it from Old High German 'dankōn', the same source as English 'thank'.

en: Please / Here you are / You're welcome
note: One word does three jobs. It is the verb 'prosić' (to ask) in the first person, so 'please' is really 'I request', and handing something over or answering thanks is also framed as a polite request.
Built from the prefix 'prze-' (through, across) and 'prosić' (to ask). Apologizing is pictured as asking your way back across a line you crossed.
'Do' (until) plus 'widzenie' (the act of seeing) in the genitive case, which 'do' always demands. The same pattern gives 'do jutra' (until tomorrow) and 'do zobaczenia' (until we see each other).

The genitive of 'smaczny' (tasty). It is the tail of 'życzę smacznego' (I wish you something tasty), with the verb dropped. Wishes in Polish take the genitive, so the ending stays even when the verb goes.
'Dobra noc' fused into one word over centuries of use. Compare 'Dobry wieczór' (good evening), which stayed two words.
From 'nauczyć' (to teach), itself from 'uczyć' with the perfective prefix 'na-'. The feminine adds '-ka', the most productive feminine suffix in Polish.

The present tense is irregular and descends from two different Proto-Indo-European roots: 'jest-' forms (cognate with English 'is') and 'być' (cognate with 'be'). Polish usually drops the pronoun because the ending already tells you who.

A worn-down form of 'szervusz', from Latin 'servus' (servant), the old Austro-Hungarian greeting 'your humble servant'. The same root gives 'servus' in Austria and 'serwus' in Poland. Works for hello and goodbye alike.

'Napot' carries the accusative ending '-t' because the day is the object of 'kívánok' (I wish). Even when people drop the verb and say just 'Jó napot', the ending stays, a fossil of the full sentence.

The '-öm' ending is the definite conjugation, used when the verb has a specific object. So the word quietly includes 'it': I thank (this specific thing). 'Köszönöm szépen' adds 'nicely' for 'thank you very much'.
Like Polish 'proszę', the verb 'kérni' (to ask for) in the first person with a definite object. 'Kérem szépen' is the polite form; 'légy szíves' (be so kind) is the informal one.

Three pieces glued together: 'viszont' (again, in return) + 'látás' (seeing) + '-ra' (onto). Hungarian builds words by stacking suffixes, which is why single words can be this long. Informally people say 'Viszlát'.
'Egészség' (health) comes from 'egész' (whole): to be healthy is to be whole. '-ed' marks 'your' and '-re' means 'onto'. Said when clinking glasses and when someone sneezes.
Hungarian has no grammatical gender at all, not even he/she ('ő' covers both). To specify a female friend you add 'nő' (woman), giving 'barátnő', which in practice usually means girlfriend.
The third person 'van' is dropped in simple 'X is Y' sentences: 'Ő tanár' means 'he/she is a teacher' with no verb at all. 'Van' reappears for location and existence.
One of the oldest words in the language, inherited from Proto-Uralic and related to Finnish 'vesi'. The long 'í' shortens when suffixes are added: 'vizet' (water, object), 'vizek' (waters).

Everyday greeting, especially in Helsinki. Usually traced to Low German or Swedish 'moin', brought by sailors and traders through the Baltic ports. 'Hei' is the neutral alternative; 'Moi moi' is goodbye.
Finnish has no everyday word for 'please'. 'Kiitos' does the job instead: 'Kahvi, kiitos' (coffee, thanks) is how you ask politely. From the verb 'kiittää' (to thank, to praise).
Both words carry the partitive ending '-ä'. Wishes in Finnish go in the partitive because you are wishing an open-ended, unmeasured amount of a good day, not one whole specific day.
From 'näkemä' (a seeing) with the plural illative ending '-iin' (into). So goodbye is 'into the seeings to come'. Compare 'kuulemiin' (goodbye on the phone, literally 'into hearings').
A case form of an old word for pardon, frozen into an interjection. The full verb is 'antaa anteeksi' (to forgive), literally 'to give into pardon'.

en: Please / You're welcome / Here you are
note: An imperative: 'be good'. Said when handing something over and as the reply to 'kiitos'. The plural or polite form is 'Olkaa hyvä'.

A very old Germanic loan, from Proto-Germanic 'kuningaz', the ancestor of English 'king'. Finnish kept the ending that the Germanic languages later wore away. The feminine suffix '-tar' gives 'kuningatar' (queen).
Finnish has no gender even in pronouns: 'hän' is he or she. The verb endings mark the person, so 'olen' alone already means 'I am'.

From 'sisä-' (inside, inner). A national idea more than a word: stubborn courage that keeps going after hope is gone. There is no single English equivalent, which is why it is usually left untranslated.

The all-purpose greeting, used with everyone from friends to the bank clerk. Doubled, 'Hei hei', it is a cheerful goodbye. Norway dropped most formal address in the 1970s, so 'hei' replaced older 'god dag' in daily life.
Norwegians thank for everything: 'takk for maten' (thanks for the food) after a meal, 'takk for sist' (thanks for last time) when you meet again. 'Tusen takk' is 'a thousand thanks'.
'Ha det' (have it) is the short form. The 'it' is your life or your time: have it good while we are apart.
'Unn-' (away, un-) plus 'skyld' (guilt, debt). Apologizing asks to be freed from a debt, the same picture as German 'Entschuldigung'.
Norwegian has no single word for please. 'Vær så snill' is a request to be kind; when offering something you say 'vær så god' (be so good) instead.
From 'kos' (cosiness, comfort). Describes candles, woollen socks, a cabin evening or a good conversation. Close cousin of Danish 'hyggelig'.
Bokmål has three genders, but person nouns are usually masculine with a feminine formed by '-inne', a suffix borrowed from Low German. 'Venninne' means a female friend, not a girlfriend ('kjæreste').
Norwegian verbs do not change for person: 'jeg er', 'du er', 'vi er' all use the same form. The work goes into tense instead. 'Er' and English 'are' are the same old word.
Said to the host when you leave the table, almost without exception. 'Maten' is 'mat' (food) with the definite article '-en' glued to the end, which is how Scandinavian languages say 'the'.

literal: welcome, (you are in) a spacious place
note: Borrowed from Arabic 'marḥaban', from the root r-ḥ-b meaning 'wide, spacious'. Greeting someone is telling them there is room for them. Turkish absorbed thousands of Arabic words through Ottoman times.

'Teşekkür' is Arabic 'tashakkur' (thanking); 'ederim' is 'I do'. Turkish often builds verbs by pairing a borrowed noun with 'etmek' (to do). The shorter 'Teşekkürler' and 'Sağ ol' (be healthy) are casual.
From Arabic 'luṭf' (kindness, grace) with the Arabic adverb ending '-an'. Turkish spells it with its own vowel harmony as 'lütfen'.
'Gün' (day) plus 'aydın' (bright, enlightened). A native Turkish compound, coined in the language reform era to replace the Arabic-Persian 'sabah-ı şerif'.
Only the person leaving says this; the person staying answers 'Güle güle'. 'Hoş' is Persian for pleasant; '-ça' makes it an adverb; 'kal' is the command 'stay'.
A doubled form of 'gülmek' (to laugh): go off laughing. The same doubling pattern gives 'yavaş yavaş' (slowly) and 'koşa koşa' (running).

en: May it come easy (said to someone working)
note: Said to anyone at work, from a shopkeeper to a road crew. 'Gelsin' is the third-person command of 'gelmek' (to come). There is no English equivalent; it acknowledges effort rather than greeting.

Turkish has no grammatical gender; 'o' means he, she and it. 'Kral' is a Slavic loan ('kralj'), ultimately from the name Charlemagne (Karl). 'Kraliçe' (queen) took the Slavic feminine ending '-ica' along with it.
Suffixes stack onto the stem 'gel-' and every vowel in them obeys vowel harmony, matching the front vowel 'e'. Present continuous '-iyor' is the everyday present tense.
From the root r-ḥ-b, 'to be wide'. The '-an' ending is the accusative 'tanwīn', which turns nouns into adverb-like exclamations. The same root is behind Turkish 'merhaba'.

'Shukr' (thanks) plus the accusative ending '-an', written with two fatḥa strokes above the final alif. Many Arabic interjections are frozen accusatives of this kind: 'ahlan' (welcome), 'ṭabʿan' (of course).

'Min' (from) + 'faḍl' (bounty, favour) + 'your'. You ask for something out of the other person's generosity. The final vowel changes with the listener's gender, which is written only in vowelled texts.

The reply is 'wa ʿalaykumu s-salām' (and upon you peace). The 'al-' of 'as-salām' assimilates to the 's' that follows, which is why it is written 'al' but pronounced 'as'. 'Salām' shares a root with 'Islam' and 'muslim': s-l-m, wholeness and peace.
Said to the person leaving: go with safety. The one leaving may answer 'Allāh yusallimak' (God keep you safe).
Three words: 'in' (if), 'shāʾa' (he willed), 'Allāh'. Used for any future plan, from the solemn to 'the bus will come, inshallah'. Often written as one word in casual Latin script.
Colloquial, from 'yā Allāh' (O God) worn down by speed. Heard across the Arab world and borrowed into Hebrew, Turkish and Greek slang.

The active participle of 'ṭalaba' (to seek, to request): a student is a seeker. The feminine adds 'tāʾ marbūṭa' (ة), the looped letter that marks almost every feminine noun. 'Taliban' is the Pashto plural of this same word.

The three-letter root k-t-b carries the idea of writing. Change the vowels and affixes and you get 'kitāb' (book), 'maktab' (office), 'maktaba' (library), 'kātib' (writer). Arabic dictionaries are organized by root, not alphabetically by word.
Sanskrit 'namas' (a bow, reverence) + 'te' (to you). The gesture of joined palms is the bow the word describes. 'Namaskār' is the slightly more formal variant.

Sanskrit 'dhanya' (blessed, fortunate) + 'vāda' (speech): to call someone blessed. A formal word; in daily life people say 'shukriyā' or simply 'thank you'. Thanking family for small things can feel oddly distant in Hindi culture.
The same Arabic root as 'shukran', arriving through Persian and Urdu. Hindi vocabulary runs on two tracks: Sanskrit-derived words like 'dhanyavād' and Perso-Arabic ones like this.
The instrumental case of Sanskrit 'kṛpā' (compassion, grace). Mostly heard in announcements and signs; in conversation politeness is carried by the verb ending '-ie' instead ('dījie', please give).
'Phir' (again) + 'milenge' (we will meet). Hindi has no dedicated word for goodbye; 'namaste' or this future-tense promise does the job.
'Māf' is Arabic 'muʿāf' (pardoned); 'kījie' is the polite command of 'karnā' (to do). The dot under फ़ marks the 'f' sound, a letter added to Devanagari for Perso-Arabic loans.
An adjective that also works as 'okay', 'I see', and with rising tone 'really?'. As an adjective it agrees with gender: 'acchā laṛkā' (good boy), 'acchī laṛkī' (good girl).
The classic masculine '-ā' / feminine '-ī' pair. Most Hindi nouns ending in '-ā' are masculine and swap to '-ī' for the feminine; adjectives follow the same rule.
Hindi has three levels of 'you': 'tū' (intimate), 'tum' (familiar), 'āp' (respectful), each with its own verb form. 'Āp' takes the plural form 'hain' even for one person, a mark of respect.

The tail of an old sentence, '今日はご機嫌いかがですか' (as for today, how are you?). Only the topic 'today' plus the particle 'wa' survived. That is why it is spelled with は (the particle) and not わ, even though it is pronounced 'wa'.
From 有り難い 'arigatai': 'ari' (to exist) + 'gatai' (difficult). A kindness is something rare, hard to come by. Add ございます for the polite form.

The negative of 済む 'sumu' (to be settled, to be finished). The feeling is that your debt to the other person is not settled. Used to get attention, to apologize, and to thank someone for trouble taken.
'O-' is an honorific prefix, 'hayō' is an old form of 早い 'hayai' (early), 'gozaimasu' is the polite 'is'. Literally praising the earliness of the hour. Friends shorten it to 'ohayō'.
From 左様なら 'sayō naraba': 'if it is that way, then...'. The rest of the sentence ('then we part') was left unsaid. It sounds final, so for 'see you later' Japanese prefer 'ja ne' or 'mata ne'.

The humble form of 'to receive', originally 'to lift above one's head', the gesture for accepting a gift from a superior. Thanks the cook, the farmer and the food itself. 'Gochisōsama' closes the meal.
'O-' (honorific) + 'tsukare' (tiredness) + 'sama' (a respectful title). You are addressing the other person's fatigue with respect. The standard sign-off among colleagues at the end of the day.

Japanese has no grammatical gender, but 'I' changes with the speaker: 'boku' is typical for men and boys, 'atashi' is feminine and casual, 'watashi' is neutral and polite. The kanji 私 also means 'private'.
A regular 'ru-verb': drop る and add endings. Japanese verbs do not change for person or number, only for tense, politeness and mood. 食 is the kanji for food, seen in 食事 (meal) and 食堂 (canteen).
'Nǐ' (you) + 'hǎo' (good). 好 is a woman 女 beside a child 子, an old picture of what is good. Two third tones in a row change the first to a rising tone, so it sounds like 'ní hǎo'.

谢 originally meant 'to decline, to excuse oneself' and drifted to 'thank'. Doubling a verb in Chinese softens it and makes it casual, so 谢谢 is lighter than 谢 alone. The second syllable loses its tone.
A verb: 'I invite you to...'. 请坐 is 'please sit', 请问 (please-ask) opens a polite question. The traditional form 請 shows the speech radical 言 beside 青.
对 (to face) + 不 (not) + 起 (rise, manage to): 'I cannot face you'. A serious apology. For small things like bumping into someone, 不好意思 (bù hǎoyìsi, 'embarrassed') is more common.
再 (again) + 见 (see), exactly parallel to French 'au revoir'. 见 is a simplified form of 見, a large eye 目 on legs.
关系 'guānxi' means relationship or connection, the famous word for personal networks. 'No connection' means 'it has no bearing, don't worry'. The reply to 对不起.
'Add fuel', as in refuelling a car or feeding a lamp. Shouted at sports events and said to friends before exams. It became so widely used that 'add oil' entered the Oxford English Dictionary in 2018.

Spoken Chinese has one word 'tā' for he, she and it. The written feminine 她 with the woman radical 女 was invented around 1920 by the poet Liu Bannong to translate Western pronouns; before that 他 covered everyone.

Chinese verbs never conjugate: 是 is the same for every person and every tense. Time is shown by context words like 昨天 (yesterday) or particles like 了. Note that adjectives do not take 是: 'I am tired' is 我很累, with no 'is'.
A folk story tells of a painter who mixed a horse and a tiger in one picture; 马虎 came to mean careless. Doubled, it means 'meh, so-so'. Four-character sayings like this are everywhere in Chinese.

From Venetian 's-ciào vostro' (your slave), a bow-and-scrape greeting like English 'your servant'. 'Schiavo' (slave) and 'Slav' share a root. Used for hello and goodbye, only with people you address as 'tu'.
The plural of 'grazia' (grace, favour), from Latin 'gratia'. 'Grazie mille' is 'a thousand thanks'. The reply is 'prego'.
First person of 'pregare' (to pray, to beg). One word for 'you're welcome', 'after you', 'please sit down' and 'sorry, what?', depending on tone.
'Buon' + 'giorno' fused. Used until early afternoon; then 'buonasera'. 'Buonanotte' is only for going to bed.

literal: until we see each other again
note: 'A' (until) + 'rivederci' (to see each other again). The formal version to one person is 'arrivederLa'.

literal: into the mouth of the wolf
note: Said before an exam or a performance, like 'break a leg'. The required answer is 'Crepi!' (may it die), never 'grazie'.
From Latin 'amicus', from 'amare' (to love). Masculine -o, feminine -a, plurals 'amici' / 'amiche' with the spelling change that keeps the 'k' sound.
'Sono' is both 'I am' and 'they are'; context decides. Italian drops subject pronouns because the ending already says who.
The h is silent: 'o-la'. Its origin is uncertain; a link to Arabic 'wa-llāh' (by God) is often claimed but not proven. Works at any time of day.
Plural of 'gracia', from Latin 'gratia'. 'Muchas gracias' is the warmer form. The reply is 'de nada'.
'Por' (by, through) + 'favor'. Spanish uses it less often than English uses 'please'; the polite verb form 'quería' or 'me pone' does the work instead.
Plural, probably short for 'buenos días os dé Dios' (may God give you good days). 'Buenas tardes' from lunchtime, 'buenas noches' after dark.
'A Dios' (to God), short for 'I commend you to God', like French 'adieu'. For a casual bye use 'hasta luego' (until later) or 'chao'.
'Sentir' is to feel; 'lo siento' means 'I feel it (your pain)'. For bumping into someone say 'perdón' or 'disculpe'.
From Latin 'amicus'. The -o/-a pair is the basic Spanish gender pattern; a mixed group is 'amigos'.
Spanish has two verbs for 'to be': 'ser' for identity and permanent traits, 'estar' for location and states. 'Soy' comes from Latin 'sum', 'eres' from 'eris'.
'Bon' + 'jour'. Say it once per person per day; a second 'bonjour' to the same person sounds odd, so people say 'rebonjour' as a joke. After about 6 pm, 'bonsoir'.
From Latin 'mercedem' (wages, reward, favour). The same word gives English 'mercy' and the phrase 'at the mercy of'. The reply is 'de rien' or 'je vous en prie'.
'Si' + 'il' + 'vous' + 'plaît' (from plaire, to please). The informal version is 's'il te plaît'. Abbreviated SVP on signs.
'Au' (to the) + 'revoir' (to see again). 'Adieu' (to God) is only for final farewells. Friends say 'salut' or 'à plus'.
'Rien' comes from Latin 'rem' (a thing), so 'nothing' in French is literally 'a thing' that negation turned inside out. 'Je vous en prie' is the formal reply.
'Ça' (that) + 'va' (goes). The answer is also 'ça va'. The space before the question mark is standard French typography.
From Latin 'amicus'. The feminine adds -e, which is silent but changes 'un ami' to 'une amie'. 'Mon amie' is used even though 'amie' is feminine, because 'ma' cannot stand before a vowel.
The circumflex marks a lost s: Old French 'estre', from Latin 'esse'. 'Es' and 'est' sound the same; only spelling tells 'tu es' from 'il est'.
The all-purpose greeting. 'Hoi' is the casual one, 'goedemorgen' / 'goedemiddag' / 'goedenavond' the polite ones by time of day. 'Dag!' works for both hello and bye.
'Dank' + 'je' (you) + 'wel' (well, indeed). The polite form is 'dank u wel'; 'bedankt' is the quick everyday version.
'Als het je belieft' squeezed into one word, exactly parallel to French 's'il te plaît'. Said when asking and when handing something over. Polite form: 'alstublieft'.
'Tot' (until) + 'ziens' (an old genitive of 'zien', to see). Casual alternatives: 'doei', 'doeg', 'later'.
From 'gezel' (companion, journeyman), the same root as German 'Geselle'. Describes a warm café, a good evening with friends, a room, a person. Famously untranslatable.
Starts with food but spreads to everything pleasant: 'lekker weer' (nice weather), 'lekker slapen' (sleep well), 'lekker bezig' (nice going, often ironic).
Cognate with English 'friend'. 'Vriendin' is a female friend and also 'girlfriend'; context decides. 'Mijn vriend' from a woman usually means boyfriend.
'Ik ben' and English 'I am' share the Germanic root; 'is' is identical in both languages. 'Zijn' is also the word for 'his'.
From Latin 'ubique' (everywhere), coined in English in the 1800s from the theological 'ubiquity' of God. Formal; collocates with 'smartphones', 'presence', 'become'.

en: to make a small supply last by careful use
note: 'Eke' is Old English 'ēcan', to increase (same root as 'nickname', from 'an eke-name'). Today it survives only in this phrasal verb: 'eke out a living', 'eke out a narrow win'.

conj.label: pattern
conj.target: eke out a living / an existence / a win

en: a question open to debate, or (US) one no longer relevant
note: 'Moot' is Old English 'gemōt', an assembly where cases were argued; law students still hold 'moot courts'. British usage: debatable. American usage: irrelevant. Often mis-spelled 'mute point'.

en: the luck of finding good things by chance
note: Coined in 1754 by Horace Walpole after the fairy tale 'The Three Princes of Serendip' (an old name for Sri Lanka), whose heroes kept making lucky discoveries. Voted one of the hardest English words to translate.
Formal and legal. 'Withstand' means to resist, so 'notwithstanding X' is 'X not resisting (this)'. Unusually, it can follow its noun: 'the weather notwithstanding'.

en: to suffer the worst part of something
literal: to carry the main force of the blow
note: 'Brunt' (the shock of an attack) is of uncertain origin, possibly Old Norse. Only ever used in this phrase: 'small businesses bore the brunt of the recession'.

en: the most perfect or typical example of something
note: Medieval alchemists added a fifth essence, aether, to earth, air, fire and water: the purest substance of all. 'The quintessential English village'. Stress on the third syllable.

en: to reduce activity gradually before stopping; to relax
note: From winding a clock or a car window. Rhymes with 'find', not 'tinned'. Separable: 'wind the business down'. Opposite 'wind up', which also means to tease someone (British).
